newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to warn chosen easterners of economic hurdles.
newsitem.headline: EU to warn chosen easterners of economic hurdles.

text.p: The European Commission will on Wednesday tell five east European countries chosen for EU membership talks that they will have to make more economic efforts before they cross the threshold.

As Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland, Slovenia and Estonia bathe in the euphoria of being recommended out of 10 east European candidates for a first wave of talks next year, they will be told bluntly that economic difficulties lie ahead.

"None of the 10 candidate countries today fulfils entirely the two economic conditions fixed (by EU leaders)...but some should be able to meet them in a few years," says a draft of the Commission's "Agenda 2000" document which maps out the challenge the EU faces into the next century.

The paper, obtained by Reuters ahead of its official release before the European Parliament on Wednesday, lists countries the Commission deems eligible for the EU's first enlargement beyond the former Iron Curtain and the policy changes the EU will have to make to accommodate them.
The changes involve a new EU inter-governmental conference soon after 2000 to overhaul the EU's decision-making procedures to prevent paralysis in a bloc with 21 members.

The EU's June 16-17 Amsterdam summit failed to agree on how to revise the way decisions are taken ahead of enlargement, but said a new overhaul would be necessary if the bloc extended to more than 20 members.
A radical reform of the EU's Common Agriculture Policy is also prescribed in the document, with drastic cuts of 10 percent in EU guaranteed prices for milk and 30 percent for cereals.
The EU executive says the EU should live under the current ceiling of the member states' financing for the first few years.

The paper, to be formally agreed by the 20 European Commissioners on Tuesday, says that all five countries chosen can be seen as having achieved functioning market economies, but their gross domestic product remains only one third of the EU average.
"In general, structural reforms have not developed enough," it said, pointing to lags in reforming the banking and financial services sectors and social security systems.

While all 10 eastern applicant countries are still struggling economically after years of communist central planning, only one -- Slovakia -- is said to have failed to make the necessary political reforms to shake off the Soviet era.
"Only one candidate, Slovakia, does not fulfil the political criteria," the document says.

The EU executive proposes that Slovakia, along with Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria and Romania, be left out of the first enlargement exercise, but placed in a cosy waiting room where they can prepare for membership at their own pace.

That proposal could be overturned by EU governments, which will have the last say. With different national interests at stake, they are expected to battle to the end of the year over the extent of the enlargement.
The Commission has also proposed that the Mediterranean island of Cyprus, which has been waiting in line for some time, be included in the first enlargement wave.
